text: Technology theme should remain decomposed around AI compute buildout, cloud infrastructure, semiconductors, optical interconnect, power/cooling, security, and automation rather than around a single mega-cap ticker.
Highest-priority underfollowed node is HBM-adjacent backend test and advanced packaging: probe cards, inspection/metrology, handlers, OSAT overflow, and semiconductor data orchestration.

Optical interconnect should be tracked down-stack into lasers, InP substrates, silicon photonics foundry, qualified epitaxy capacity, and epitaxy tools rather than only transceiver or networking leaders.

Semiconductor manufacturing orchestration software is a non-obvious data-layer node linking fabless, foundry, OSAT, test, and equipment workflows; PDF Solutions is the current cleanest Layer 1 candidate.

Data-center power, cooling, water, electrical distribution, cabling, and component suppliers remain relevant second-order AI infrastructure nodes but need a broader candidate search beyond Vertiv and Eaton.
AI cybersecurity, identity, observability, and automation software should remain in the funnel as low-confidence hypotheses requiring product-level and revenue-level evidence.

Layer 2 must collect primary-source filings, investor presentations, transcripts, current market caps, liquidity, analyst coverage, customer concentration, and valuation checks before promoting any Layer 1C candidate.

Non-US listings are essential for this theme because several chokepoint suppliers sit in Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and Europe; dashboard symbol normalization and ADR/local-listing deduplication are required.

Technology theme currently maps most cleanly into AI infrastructure chokepoints: AI servers and accelerators pull through HBM, advanced packaging, backend test, MLCCs, specialty glass, optical interconnect, and manufacturing orchestration software.

Highest-priority potential bottleneck nodes are upstream MLCC dielectric powders, high-end AI-server MLCCs, T-glass / specialty glass cloth, HBM-adjacent backend test, and advanced packaging capacity.

Low-attention bottleneck value may hide one or two layers below the obvious AI leaders: ceramic powders below MLCC makers, glass cloth below substrates, epitaxy tools below optical modules, and test/probe infrastructure below HBM producers.
2026-2027 advanced-glass capacity expansion is a key catalyst and falsification event: tight utilization after expansion would support the bottleneck thesis, while rapid oversupply would weaken it.

Customer validation and yield milestones for FOPLP / panel-level packaging are important catalysts for whether Powertech-like memory backend providers become AI/HPC advanced-packaging nodes rather than only conventional memory OSATs.
Follow-on HBM-related inspection, metrology, test-handler, and probe-card orders are the key catalyst class for test-equipment and test-interface suppliers.

Primary-source verification is still needed for Substack-sourced claims on Sakai Chemical share, sub-100nm BaTiO3 supplier concentration, Powertech price hikes, AMD/Broadcom FOPLP backing, and the unnamed T-glass supplier's market share and capacity expansion.

For each mapped public company, next layers should check filings, earnings transcripts, segment revenue, capex, backlog, customer concentration, product qualification, and margin evidence before scoring investability.

Distribution and allocation channels remain an unverified but plausible hidden node for passive components and optical components; current evidence is insufficient, so this should remain hypothesis-level.
Mega-cap GPU, cloud, and memory leaders should be treated as demand causers or reference customers in this funnel, not as the main Layer 2A bottleneck nodes.

PDFS should be tracked as an underfollowed semiconductor manufacturing orchestration hypothesis, not as a direct AI chip supplier. Key survival evidence is product-level adoption by OSATs, advanced packaging providers, HBM suppliers, or fabless/foundry ecosystems.
FORM maps most cleanly to the HBM and advanced-packaging wafer-test interface chokepoint. Prioritize DRAM probe-card mix, HBM design wins, capacity utilization, and margin evidence.

COHU maps to HBM-related backend inspection, metrology, test handlers, contactors, and automation. Thesis should be downgraded if HBM/AI orders are one-off or immaterial relative to cyclical semiconductor test recovery.

AXTI is a speculative underfollowed InP substrate candidate for AI optical interconnect. Survival depends on visible datacenter optical demand, customer qualifications, and evidence that substrate supply rather than module assembly is the constraint.

AIXA.DE is an underfollowed epitaxy-tool candidate beneath the optical/laser expansion layer. Separate AI optical demand from power-electronics and broader compound-semiconductor cyclicality before promotion.

6239.TW has one of the more interesting Serenity structures in this chunk: memory backend overflow plus FOPLP/PiFO advanced packaging optionality. However, current evidence is still secondary-heavy and needs official filings, revenue, yield, pricing, and customer validation.

LITE remains an optical-interconnect inference. Track whether AI datacenter optical demand is translating into laser capacity utilization and durable revenue rather than a temporary transceiver cycle.

COHR should be treated as an optical supply-chain reference anchor, useful for benchmarking laser/material demand and InP capacity, but not allowed to crowd out smaller substrate, equipment, or niche suppliers.

FN should be treated as an assembly/manufacturing benchmark for optical modules and datacenter photonics. It is useful to test whether scarcity sits in precision manufacturing or further upstream in lasers, substrates, and epitaxy tools.

Primary-source evidence is missing for most non-Powertech candidate relationships in this chunk. Next Layer 2C should gather filings, transcripts, product disclosures, customer concentration, order intake, and segment exposure before upgrading any relationship to fact.

Market-cap buckets and liquidity should be refreshed before Layer 3, especially for non-US listings and volatile optical/test equipment names. Current labels are inherited from cached Layer 1 and not independently refreshed in this Layer 2B output.
MTSI mapped to optical interconnect, signal integrity, and datacenter photonics components as an underfollowed hypothesis; evidence gap is company-level AI optical revenue and design-win proof.
SMTC mapped to signal-integrity and optical connectivity components; the key issue is whether datacenter/AI optical demand is large enough relative to Semtech's broader analog and IoT businesses.
5803.T mapped to AI data-center fiber, cabling, and physical connectivity; requires Japanese primary-source verification of datacenter revenue, capacity constraints, and hyperscale exposure.
VRT retained as reference anchor for AI data-center power, cooling, and thermal-management demand; use to benchmark smaller power and cooling suppliers rather than as an underfollowed candidate.
CLS mapped to AI data-center hardware, networking systems, and electronics manufacturing; requires verification of AI/networking program exposure, customer concentration, and margin sustainability.
CLS.TO is a cross-listing/alias for Celestica and should be deduplicated against CLS in the dashboard security master.
ETN retained as reference anchor for data-center electrical infrastructure and power-management demand; likely too widely followed and diversified for the underfollowed lane.
POWL mapped to electrical distribution and control systems as an underfollowed data-center power infrastructure hypothesis; key survival test is data-center backlog or customer proof.

ATKR mapped to electrical raceway, conduit, and cable-management components as a second-order AI data-center construction beneficiary; must test whether AI demand offsets construction cyclicality and channel risks.
BMI retained only as speculative shadow exposure to cooling-loop flow measurement, water instrumentation, or utility water infrastructure serving data centers.

This chunk has weak primary-source evidence. Before Layer 3 promotion, gather filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, segment revenue, customer concentration, and backlog/order data for each underfollowed candidate.

Separate AI-specific demand from broad cyclical recovery for MTSI, SMTC, Fujikura, Celestica, Powell, Atkore, and Badger Meter. Require explicit AI, hyperscale, datacenter, 800G/1.6T, liquid cooling, electrical infrastructure, or mission-critical facility evidence.

IOT maps to edge operational data and industrial AI data nodes as a speculative-shadow second-order AI candidate; current official evidence supports strong ARR growth, large-customer expansion, emerging-product contribution, and a large proprietary physical-operations dataset, but not yet standalone AI monetization.

PATH maps to enterprise AI automation and agentic workflow orchestration nodes; official evidence supports product-level agentic AI positioning, AI-agent security certification, and Azure AI Foundry integration, but the chokepoint thesis remains unproven until ARR acceleration and retention effects are visible.

For IOT, next layer should separate base connected-operations growth from AI-driven incremental economics by tracking emerging-products ACV mix, AI product attach rate, net retention, product gross margin, and customer expansion case studies.

For PATH, next layer should test whether agentic automation is reviving the RPA growth curve or merely slowing decline by reviewing Q1 FY27 official disclosures, AI deal mix, AI expansion deal size, customer production deployments, churn, and competitive displacement data.

Neither IOT nor PATH should be promoted as a Serenity bottleneck candidate until primary filings or transcripts show AI-specific revenue pull-through, pricing power, retention lift, or workflow lock-in that cannot be easily replicated by larger software platforms.
